stem: A team is designing Direct Connect connectivity for a mission-critical workload and needs the configuration that the AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit recommends for the highest connection SLA (99.99%), by terminating separate connections on separate devices in more than one Direct Connect location. Which configuration matches this recommendation?
options: Four connections that terminate on separate devices, spread across two or more Direct Connect locations.
A single connection at one Direct Connect location, optionally placed in a LAG to increase throughput.
Two connections, each terminating on a different device, but both within the same Direct Connect location.
Two connections, one at each of two Direct Connect locations, each using a single device per location.
explanation: The Maximum resiliency model uses separate connections that terminate on separate devices in more than one location (a minimum of four connections across two or more locations) and is the only Resiliency Toolkit model that achieves the 99.99% SLA while protecting against device, connectivity, and complete location failure at the same time. A single connection has no built-in redundancy at all. Two connections on separate devices within one location is the Development and Test model, which protects against device failure but not location failure and does not reach the higher SLA tiers. One connection per location, one device each, is the High Resiliency model, which achieves the 99.9% SLA rather than 99.99%.

stem: A media company is designing a transit gateway architecture that must deliver multicast video streams to receivers in several attached VPCs, while a subset of receivers sit at an on-premises data center reached over an existing Direct Connect connection. Which design constraint must the team account for regarding transit gateway multicast?
options: Transit gateway multicast automatically tunnels multicast traffic over any Direct Connect virtual interface without extra configuration.

Transit gateway multicast can route multicast traffic between subnets in attached VPCs, but multicast routing is not supported over Direct Connect, Site-to-Site VPN, peering attachments, or Connect attachments, so on-premises receivers need a different distribution method.
Transit gateway multicast requires every receiving instance to use a non-Nitro instance type to join a multicast group.
Transit gateway multicast can be enabled on any existing transit gateway at any time without recreating it.
explanation: Transit gateway multicast routes traffic only between subnets in attached VPCs, and multicast routing is explicitly not supported over Direct Connect, Site-to-Site VPN, peering attachments, or Connect attachments, so the on-premises receivers need a separate distribution mechanism rather than native transit gateway multicast. Multicast is not automatically tunneled over Direct Connect; it is unsupported there entirely. Non-Nitro instances cannot even act as multicast senders and must have source/destination checking disabled, the opposite of being required for every receiver. A new transit gateway must be created specifically to support multicast; it cannot be enabled retroactively on an existing one.

stem: A company peers three transit gateways in a chain: TGW-A is peered with TGW-B, and TGW-B is peered with TGW-C. A VPC attached to TGW-A needs to reach a VPC attached to TGW-C. Which TWO statements correctly describe the design implications of transit gateway peering in this scenario? (Select TWO.)
options: Traffic from the VPC on TGW-A can reach the VPC on TGW-C automatically through TGW-B, because transit gateway peering supports transitive routing.
Transit gateway peering does not support transitive routing, so a direct peering attachment between TGW-A and TGW-C is required for that traffic to flow.
Routes to a peering attachment are added automatically through dynamic route propagation, so no static routes are needed in the transit gateway route tables.
Routes to a peering attachment must be added as static routes in each transit gateway's route table; dynamic route propagation is not used over peering attachments.
Inter-Region transit gateway peering traffic is sent unencrypted across the AWS backbone between Regions.
explanation: Transit gateway peering is not transitive: a VPC on TGW-A cannot reach a VPC on TGW-C just because TGW-A peers with TGW-B and TGW-B peers with TGW-C, so a direct peering attachment between TGW-A and TGW-C is required. Routing over a peering attachment also always uses static routes added to each transit gateway route table, since peering attachments do not support dynamic route propagation. The transitive-routing option is the opposite of how peering behaves, and automatic dynamic propagation over peering attachments does not exist. Inter-Region peering traffic is encrypted with AES-256 at the virtual network layer (and again at the physical layer outside AWS's control), so it is not sent unencrypted.

stem: A company centralizes networking in a shared-services account and wants every VPC in dozens of member accounts to resolve a corporate domain hosted on-premises, without configuring a separate DNS forwarder in every account. Which design achieves this with the least ongoing per-account effort?
options: In each member account, deploy a separate Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and a duplicate forwarding rule pointing to the on-premises DNS servers.
Configure a Route 53 private hosted zone in every member account that duplicates the on-premises DNS records.

In the shared-services account, create one Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and one forwarding rule for the domain, then share the rule using AWS Resource Access Manager so member accounts can associate it with their own VPCs.
Attach a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint to every VPC that needs to query the on-premises domain.
explanation: Route 53 Resolver forwarding rules can be created once in a central account and shared through AWS RAM, so each member account only has to associate the shared rule with its own VPCs, avoiding duplicated outbound endpoints and rules everywhere. Deploying a separate outbound endpoint and rule in every account duplicates the same configuration repeatedly. Manually duplicating DNS records in a private hosted zone creates an ongoing synchronization burden and is not how conditional forwarding works. An inbound endpoint accepts queries arriving from on-premises into the VPC; it is the wrong direction for VPC resources querying an on-premises name, which needs an outbound endpoint.

stem: A company has a primary Direct Connect private virtual interface and a backup private virtual interface to the same VPC, and wants inbound traffic from AWS to always prefer the primary path unless it fails, without changing AS_PATH prepending. Which BGP community tag design achieves this active/passive behavior?
options: Apply the same local preference community, such as 7224:7200, to the prefixes on both virtual interfaces so traffic load-balances across them.
Apply the NO_EXPORT community to the primary virtual interface only.
Rely on Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) values instead of any local preference community tag, since MED is evaluated before AS_PATH.
Apply a higher local preference community, such as 7224:7300, to the prefixes advertised on the primary virtual interface, and a lower one, such as 7224:7100, on the backup virtual interface.
explanation: Direct Connect local preference BGP communities let you set a higher-preference tag (7224:7300) on the primary virtual interface and a lower-preference tag (7224:7100) on the backup virtual interface to build deterministic active/passive failover, and local preference is evaluated before AS_PATH. Applying the same community to both interfaces is the active/active load-balancing pattern, the opposite of what is needed here. NO_EXPORT only limits how far a route propagates beyond the Amazon network and has no effect on active/passive preference. AWS does not recommend relying on MED for this, and MED is in fact evaluated after prefix length, local preference, and AS_PATH, making it a weak, low-priority mechanism for this purpose.

stem: A network team wants to own and centrally manage the VPCs, route tables, and network ACLs for the whole company, while individual application teams in their own AWS accounts deploy EC2 instances and RDS databases into the appropriate subnets without needing their own VPCs. Which design meets this goal?
options: Have the network team share specific subnets from its VPC using AWS Resource Access Manager with the application team accounts (participants) in the same AWS Organizations organization.
Give every application team account a VPC peering connection to the network team's VPC.
Have every application team create its own VPC and connect to the network team's VPC over a transit gateway.
Grant application teams IAM permissions to modify the network team's VPC directly using cross-account roles.
explanation: VPC subnet sharing through AWS RAM lets an owner account share specific subnets with participant accounts in the same organization; participants can then deploy their own resources (EC2, RDS, Lambda, and so on) directly into the shared subnets, while the owner retains control of the VPC itself, its route tables, and its NACLs, and participants cannot view or modify other participants' or the owner's resources. Peering and a transit gateway design both still require every application team to run its own VPC, exactly the operational overhead the network team wants to avoid. Granting cross-account IAM roles to modify the owner's VPC breaks the centralized-ownership model the network team wants to keep.

stem: A team enables IPv6 for a VPC and wants instances in a private subnet to initiate outbound IPv6 connections to the internet, while preventing the internet from initiating inbound IPv6 connections to those instances. A NAT gateway is already used for IPv4 outbound access. Which component should the team add for IPv6?
options: A second NAT gateway configured specifically for IPv6 traffic.
An egress-only internet gateway, with a route for ::/0 pointing to it in the subnet's route table.
A standard internet gateway attached directly to the private subnet's route table for ::/0.
A Direct Connect public virtual interface to reach IPv6 destinations.
explanation: An egress-only internet gateway is the IPv6 equivalent of a NAT gateway for outbound-only access: it lets private-subnet instances initiate outbound IPv6 traffic while blocking internet-initiated inbound connections, and it is enabled with a ::/0 route in the subnet's route table. NAT gateways are an IPv4-only construct and do not support IPv6. Attaching a standard internet gateway directly would make the subnet's IPv6 addresses reachable from the internet, since IPv6 addresses are globally routable by default, defeating the goal. A Direct Connect public virtual interface is for hybrid connectivity to AWS public endpoints, not general internet access control.

stem: A multiplayer gaming company runs a UDP-based matchmaking service in two AWS Regions and needs a fixed set of entry-point IP addresses, fast failover to the healthy Region, and traffic carried over the AWS global network rather than the public internet. Which service is the BEST fit?
options: Amazon CloudFront, because it caches content at edge locations closest to players.
Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing alone, without any accelerator.
AWS Global Accelerator, using static anycast IP addresses that route traffic onto the AWS global network and fail over automatically between healthy endpoints.
An Application Load Balancer in a single Region with cross-zone load balancing enabled.
explanation: AWS Global Accelerator provides fixed anycast static IP addresses that bring traffic onto the AWS global network at the nearest edge location, supports non-HTTP protocols such as UDP, and performs automatic health-check-based failover across Regional endpoints, matching every requirement in the stem. CloudFront is an HTTP/S content-delivery cache, not a fit for a UDP matchmaking protocol. Route 53 latency-based routing alone still relies on DNS TTLs for failover and does not carry traffic over the AWS backbone. A single-Region Application Load Balancer provides no multi-Region failover and, as an HTTP(S) load balancer, is not intended for UDP matchmaking traffic either.

stem: A team needs more aggregate throughput between an on-premises network and a transit gateway than a single Site-to-Site VPN tunnel provides, and wants to scale bandwidth by spreading traffic across multiple tunnels. Which design is required to achieve this with equal-cost multi-path routing?
options: Configure static routes on every VPN connection, since ECMP works only with static routing.
Create a single VPN connection and rely on its two tunnels alone, since ECMP does not apply across separate VPN connections.
Increase the instance size of the customer gateway device, which automatically enables ECMP across tunnels.
Establish multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections to the transit gateway using BGP (dynamic routing) with matching AS_PATH length and attributes, so traffic can be spread across all tunnels using ECMP.
explanation: Equal-cost multi-path routing across VPN tunnels requires BGP dynamic routing so that multiple tunnels, across one or more VPN connections, can present routes with the same AS_PATH length and attributes for the transit gateway to load-balance across; this is also how AWS documents scaling beyond a single Large Bandwidth Tunnel's cap by adding more VPN connections. Static routing does not support ECMP in this way. A single VPN connection's two tunnels exist for tunnel redundancy, not as the mechanism for scaling bandwidth beyond one connection; ECMP explicitly extends across multiple VPN connections. Customer gateway instance size has no bearing on whether ECMP is enabled.

stem: A network team manages dozens of route tables and security groups across many accounts that all reference the same set of corporate office CIDR ranges. The ranges change periodically, and updating every route table and security group by hand is error-prone. Which design BEST reduces this operational burden?
options: Create a customer-managed prefix list containing the office CIDR ranges, share it using AWS Resource Access Manager, and reference the prefix list ID in route tables and security group rules instead of individual CIDRs.
Create a separate AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory to store the CIDR ranges as attributes.
Use AWS Config rules to automatically rewrite security group CIDR entries whenever they drift from a baseline.
Store the CIDR ranges in an Amazon S3 object and have every route table poll the object for changes.
explanation: A customer-managed prefix list centralizes a reusable set of CIDR blocks; updating the prefix list once propagates the change everywhere it is referenced in route tables and security group rules, and it can be shared across accounts through AWS RAM for consistent multi-account management. AWS Managed Microsoft AD stores directory objects, not network CIDR configuration. AWS Config can detect and report drift but does not natively rewrite security group CIDR entries as a design pattern for this problem. Route tables and security groups do not poll S3 objects; there is no such native mechanism.

stem: A security team wants to insert third-party firewall appliances transparently in front of many application VPCs, with the appliances centrally managed and scaled independently of the applications, and with traffic inspection kept within the same Availability Zone to avoid cross-AZ charges and latency. Which design is BEST?
options: Deploy the firewall appliances directly in each application VPC's public subnet and update each application team's route tables individually.

Deploy the firewall appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer in a central inspection VPC, and create a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint in each application VPC's subnet in the matching Availability Zone, with route table entries directing traffic through the endpoint.
Attach a Network Firewall directly to each application VPC's internet gateway with no endpoints required.
Run the firewall appliances as targets behind an Application Load Balancer in the inspection VPC and use VPC peering to route traffic to it.
explanation: Gateway Load Balancer centralizes the appliance fleet in an inspection VPC, and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints deployed in each application VPC's subnet, matched to the same Availability Zone as the load balancer, let route tables transparently redirect traffic through the endpoint using GENEVE encapsulation on UDP port 6081, avoiding cross-AZ traffic. Deploying appliances into every application VPC abandons central management and does not scale independently. Network Firewall integrates through firewall subnets and route tables, not by attaching directly to an internet gateway with no endpoints. An Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 for HTTP(S) targets, not the load-balancing tier that transparent GWLB-based appliance insertion uses, and VPC peering does not carry GENEVE-encapsulated GWLB traffic the way a GWLB endpoint does.

stem: A company has a single Direct Connect connection in one Region and transit gateways with VPC attachments in that Region and in a second Region. The team wants on-premises to reach VPCs in both Regions using only the existing single Direct Connect connection. Which design achieves this?
options: Order a second, dedicated Direct Connect connection terminating in the second Region.
Create a VPC peering connection between the transit gateways in the two Regions.
Attach a transit virtual interface to a Direct Connect gateway, and associate the Direct Connect gateway with the transit gateway in each Region, configuring allowed prefixes for each association.
Enable a Site-to-Site VPN connection from on-premises directly into the second Region's transit gateway as the only path to that Region.
explanation: A Direct Connect gateway is a globally available, distributed resource: associating it with a transit virtual interface on the existing connection and then associating the gateway with a transit gateway in each Region (with allowed prefixes configured per association) lets a single Direct Connect connection reach VPCs across multiple Regions. Ordering a second physical connection is unnecessary extra cost and defeats the single-connection requirement. Transit gateways cannot be linked using VPC peering; that is a distinct feature (transit gateway peering attachments) and does not apply here. Adding a separate VPN into the second Region does not use the existing Direct Connect connection at all.

stem: A team wants to combine multiple existing Direct Connect connections into a single logical, higher-bandwidth connection using a Link Aggregation Group (LAG). Which combination of connections can be placed into one LAG?
options: Two 10 Gbps connections that terminate on two different Direct Connect devices in the same location.
A 10 Gbps connection and a 1 Gbps connection that both terminate on the same Direct Connect device.
Five 1 Gbps connections that all terminate on the same Direct Connect device.
Four 1 Gbps connections that all terminate on the same Direct Connect device and use the same bandwidth.
explanation: A LAG requires all connections to terminate at the same Direct Connect device (endpoint), use the same bandwidth, and is limited to a maximum of four connections below 100 Gbps (or two connections at 100/400 Gbps), so four matching 1 Gbps connections on the same device is valid. Connections on two different devices cannot join the same LAG, since AWS prevents connections used for device-level resiliency from being combined into a single LAG. Mixing 10 Gbps and 1 Gbps connections violates the same-bandwidth rule. Five connections below the 100 Gbps tier exceeds the four-connection maximum for that speed tier.

stem: A company needs remote employees to connect over a VPN into a specific application subnet, using X.509 client certificates for endpoint trust, and then restricting which employees can reach that subnet based on their Active Directory group membership. Which Client VPN configuration achieves both requirements?
options: Configure the Client VPN endpoint with mutual authentication using a server and client certificate chain, combined with Active Directory authentication, and add an authorization rule that grants only the required AD group access to the target subnet's CIDR.
Configure the Client VPN endpoint with mutual authentication only, and rely on the VPC's security groups alone to restrict which employees can reach the subnet.
Configure the Client VPN endpoint with federated (SAML) authentication only, since combining it with mutual authentication is not supported.
Skip authorization rules entirely and rely only on the network ACL of the target subnet to restrict access by AD group.
explanation: Client VPN supports combining mutual (certificate-based) authentication with Active Directory or federated authentication, and authorization rules map a user group, such as an AD group, to a specific target network CIDR, which is exactly how to layer certificate-based trust with group-based access restriction. Relying on security groups alone does not use Client VPN's built-in group-to-network authorization model and conflates network-layer filtering with user-identity-based access. Combining mutual authentication with federated or Active Directory authentication is explicitly supported, so that combination is not disallowed. Network ACLs operate on IP ranges, not AD group identity, so they cannot enforce group-based authorization by themselves.

stem: A team must let resources in a VPC resolve a domain that is authoritative on an on-premises DNS server reachable over an existing Direct Connect connection. Which set of Route 53 Resolver components must the team configure in the VPC's account?
options: A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint only, since inbound endpoints handle all DNS forwarding in both directions.

A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with elastic network interfaces in at least two Availability Zones, plus a forwarding rule for the on-premises domain that points to the on-premises DNS server IP addresses, associated with the VPC.
A public Route 53 hosted zone that duplicates the on-premises domain's records.
A Direct Connect public virtual interface dedicated to DNS traffic.
explanation: Resolving an on-premises domain from within a VPC requires an outbound Resolver endpoint (with ENIs across multiple Availability Zones for availability) and a forwarding (conditional) rule for that domain pointing at the on-premises DNS server IPs, associated with the VPC; traffic then flows over the existing private connection. An inbound endpoint handles the opposite direction: queries arriving from on-premises into the VPC's Resolver, not from the VPC out to on-premises. A duplicated public hosted zone requires ongoing manual synchronization and does not reflect live on-premises records. Direct Connect virtual interfaces have no dedicated DNS-traffic VIF type; DNS queries simply ride over the existing private connection.

stem: A security vendor wants to offer a centralized traffic-inspection appliance as a service that other AWS accounts can insert transparently into their own VPCs, without exposing the appliance fleet's IP addresses or requiring the consumer accounts to peer with the vendor's VPC. Which implementation is correct?
options: The vendor creates a Network Load Balancer and shares its DNS name directly with consumer accounts to call over the internet.
The vendor creates a VPC peering connection to every consumer account and routes traffic to the appliances through the peering connection.

The vendor fronts the appliance fleet with a Gateway Load Balancer, creates a VPC endpoint service backed by that Gateway Load Balancer, and consumer accounts create Gateway Load Balancer endpoints that connect to the service through AWS PrivateLink.
The vendor publishes the appliance fleet's private IP addresses so consumer accounts can add static routes directly to the appliance instances.
explanation: A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint service, built with AWS PrivateLink, lets a provider front an appliance fleet with a Gateway Load Balancer and expose it as a service; consumer accounts create their own Gateway Load Balancer endpoints that connect privately to the service without the provider exposing appliance IP addresses or requiring VPC peering. Sharing an NLB DNS name over the internet exposes the service publicly and forgoes PrivateLink's private connectivity model. VPC peering to every consumer does not scale and is not how PrivateLink-based service sharing works. Publishing raw private IP addresses for static routing exposes internal appliance addressing and bypasses the endpoint-service model entirely.

stem: A team has three VPCs (Prod, Shared-Services, and Dev) and creates two VPC peering connections: Prod-to-Shared-Services and Shared-Services-to-Dev. Which TWO statements correctly describe the limitations of this design? (Select TWO.)
options: Traffic from Prod can already reach Dev through Shared-Services without any extra configuration, because VPC peering is transitive.
A new, direct VPC peering connection between Prod and Dev is unnecessary as long as both existing peering connections remain active.
Prod and Dev can be peered directly even if their IPv4 CIDR blocks overlap with each other.

If Shared-Services has a NAT gateway or a Direct Connect connection, Dev cannot use it through the Shared-Services-to-Dev peering connection, because VPC peering does not support edge-to-edge routing through a peered VPC.
To let Prod reach Dev directly, a separate VPC peering connection must be created between Prod and Dev, because peering relationships are not transitive.
explanation: VPC peering is never transitive, so Prod cannot reach Dev through Shared-Services without a separate, direct peering connection between Prod and Dev. Peering also does not support edge-to-edge routing: a VPC cannot use another peered VPC's NAT gateway, internet gateway, VPN, or Direct Connect connection to reach beyond it. The transitive-routing claim and the claim that both existing connections remaining active is enough are both false for the same non-transitive reason. Overlapping CIDR blocks are explicitly disallowed for a new peering connection, so Prod and Dev could not even be peered directly if their CIDRs overlapped.

stem: A team runs private subnets in three Availability Zones and wants outbound internet access for those subnets to keep working even if one Availability Zone has a problem, while avoiding unnecessary cross-AZ data transfer charges during normal operation. Which NAT gateway design is BEST?
options: Deploy a single NAT gateway in one Availability Zone and route all three private subnets' default traffic to it.
Deploy one NAT gateway per Region instead of per Availability Zone, since NAT gateways are Region-scoped resources.
Deploy two NAT gateways in the same Availability Zone for redundancy, and route all subnets to whichever is cheaper.
Deploy one NAT gateway in each of the three Availability Zones, and route each private subnet's default route to the NAT gateway in its own Availability Zone.
explanation: One NAT gateway per Availability Zone, with each subnet's default route pointing to the NAT gateway in the same AZ, keeps outbound traffic local to the zone, avoiding cross-AZ data transfer charges, and means an AZ-level issue only affects that AZ's own NAT gateway rather than the whole VPC. A single NAT gateway in one AZ is a single point of failure and forces cross-AZ traffic from the other two AZs. NAT gateways are created within a specific subnet in a specific Availability Zone, not deployed as one Region-wide resource. Placing two NAT gateways in the same AZ still leaves the whole design exposed if that one AZ has a problem.

stem: A company wants to enable MACsec (802.1AE) encryption on an existing Direct Connect connection for wire-speed, point-to-point encryption between their router and the AWS Direct Connect device. Which implementation requirement applies?
options: MACsec is available only on dedicated connections at MACsec-capable ports and locations, and requires associating a Connectivity Association Key (CAK) and Connectivity Association Key Name (CKN) pair with the connection.
MACsec can be enabled on any hosted connection provided by an AWS Direct Connect Partner, with no location restrictions.
MACsec replaces the need for BGP authentication, so no CAK/CKN key association is required.
MACsec is configured entirely within the customer's on-premises router and requires no configuration on the AWS side of the connection.
explanation: MACsec on Direct Connect is supported only on dedicated connections at MACsec-capable ports and locations, and is enabled by associating a CAK/CKN key pair with the connection (or with a LAG, where only one key is active across all LAG links at a time). It is not available on hosted connections. MACsec operates at the Ethernet (Layer 2) frame level and is independent of BGP peer authentication, so it does not replace BGP authentication. Because MACsec secures the physical link between the customer router and the AWS Direct Connect device, both sides must be configured, including key association on the AWS side, in addition to the customer router.

stem: A team creates an interface VPC endpoint for an AWS service so that applications already coded to call the service's standard public DNS hostname (as used by the AWS SDK) transparently resolve to the endpoint's private IP addresses instead of the public endpoint. Which configuration is required?
options: Disable DNS resolution and DNS hostnames for the VPC, since private DNS names bypass VPC DNS settings entirely.
Enable the endpoint's private DNS name option, and ensure the VPC has both DNS hostnames and DNS resolution enabled.
Manually create a public Route 53 hosted zone that overrides the AWS service's public hostname for the whole internet.
Configure a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint, since private DNS names for interface endpoints depend on inbound endpoints.
explanation: Enabling an interface endpoint's private DNS name option, together with the VPC's DNS hostnames and DNS resolution attributes both enabled, makes the standard public service hostname resolve to the endpoint's private IPs for resources inside the VPC, so existing SDK code needs no changes. Disabling the VPC's DNS attributes is the opposite of what is required, since private DNS resolution depends on those attributes being enabled. Overriding a hostname in a public Route 53 hosted zone would incorrectly affect resolution for the entire internet, not just the VPC. Resolver inbound endpoints handle queries arriving from outside the VPC and are unrelated to how an interface endpoint's private DNS name resolves for resources inside the VPC.

stem: A team is implementing IPv6 outbound-only access for a private subnet. After associating an IPv6 CIDR block with the VPC and allocating a /64 IPv6 range to the subnet, which route table entry correctly completes the implementation?
options: A route for the subnet's own IPv6 CIDR pointing to a NAT gateway.
A route for 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the egress-only internet gateway.
A route for ::/0 pointing to the egress-only internet gateway.
A route for ::/0 pointing to a standard internet gateway.
explanation: Outbound-only IPv6 internet access needs a route for ::/0 (all IPv6 destinations) pointing to the egress-only internet gateway in the subnet's route table, alongside the local routes for the VPC's own CIDR blocks. Routing the subnet's own CIDR to a NAT gateway does not make sense for outbound-to-internet traffic, and NAT gateways are IPv4-only besides. 0.0.0.0/0 is the IPv4 default-route syntax, not IPv6. Routing ::/0 to a standard internet gateway would make the subnet's globally routable IPv6 addresses reachable from the internet, defeating the outbound-only requirement.

stem: Account Z owns a Direct Connect gateway. Account A owns a transit gateway with several VPC attachments and wants to use Account Z's Direct Connect gateway to reach on-premises. Which sequence correctly implements this cross-account association?
options: Account Z creates the transit gateway attachment directly inside Account A's account, bypassing any proposal step.
Account A shares its transit gateway with Account Z using AWS RAM, and Account Z attaches VPCs directly to it.
Account Z sends an association proposal to Account A, and Account A must accept it before traffic can flow.

Account A sends an association proposal for its transit gateway to Account Z, Account Z accepts the proposal and can optionally adjust the allowed prefixes, and only then can traffic route between Account A's transit gateway and Account Z's Direct Connect gateway.
explanation: For a cross-account Direct Connect gateway association, the owner of the transit gateway (Account A) sends the association proposal to the Direct Connect gateway owner (Account Z), who must accept it (and can adjust the allowed prefixes) before routing works; Account Z, as the gateway owner, retains routing ownership to the customer. The proposal flows from the transit gateway owner to the gateway owner, not the reverse. Account Z cannot unilaterally create the attachment inside Account A's account; the transit gateway owner must initiate the proposal. Sharing a transit gateway through AWS RAM for VPC attachments is a different mechanism than a Direct Connect gateway association proposal and does not match this scenario.

stem: Before sending any live traffic, a network engineer wants to verify whether a planned path between an EC2 instance and an RDS instance in another subnet will succeed, and if not, learn exactly which component (such as a security group or route table) is blocking it. Which tool BEST fits this need?
options: VPC Reachability Analyzer, which performs a static configuration analysis and reports hop-by-hop path details or identifies the specific blocking component.
VPC Flow Logs, which record only after live traffic has already been sent.
AWS X-Ray, which traces application-level requests inside already-running services.
Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries, which run scripted browser or API requests against public endpoints.
explanation: Reachability Analyzer performs a configuration-only analysis (it does not send live packets) between a source and destination, and it returns either a successful hop-by-hop path or identifies the specific blocking security group, network ACL, route table, or load balancer configuration, exactly matching the before-sending-traffic requirement. Flow Logs only reveal what already happened to real traffic that was sent, the opposite of a pre-traffic check. X-Ray traces application-level requests inside running services, not network path configuration. CloudWatch Synthetics tests public endpoint availability with real requests, not a static configuration analysis of internal network paths.

stem: A security engineer sees REJECT entries in VPC Flow Logs for traffic between two EC2 instances in the same VPC and wants to identify the exact rule that is blocking the traffic. Which TWO statements about diagnosing this are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: VPC Flow Logs records show whether traffic was ACCEPTED or REJECTED, but do not identify which specific security group or network ACL rule caused a REJECT.
VPC Reachability Analyzer performs a static configuration analysis and can identify the specific security group, network ACL, or route table entry that is blocking the path between the two instances.
Flow Logs can only be published to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, so Amazon Athena cannot be used to query them.
A REJECT entry in Flow Logs always means a network ACL rule is blocking the traffic, never a security group.
Enabling VPC Flow Logs requires installing a monitoring agent on every EC2 instance in the VPC.
explanation: Flow Logs record only ACCEPT or REJECT for each flow and do not identify which specific rule caused a REJECT, whereas Reachability Analyzer performs a static configuration analysis and can pinpoint the exact security group, network ACL, or route table entry responsible, making the two tools complementary for this diagnosis. Flow Logs can be published to Amazon S3 and Amazon Data Firehose as well as CloudWatch Logs, and Athena is a documented way to query S3-based flow log data, so the CloudWatch-only claim is false. A REJECT can come from either a security group or a network ACL, so it never being a security group is false. Flow Logs are collected at the network interface level using the underlying infrastructure; no agent installation on instances is required.

stem: A company operates transit gateways in many Regions, several Direct Connect connections, Site-to-Site VPN connections, and on-premises sites, and wants one central, visual topology and event-monitoring view across all of them. Which AWS capability BEST fits this need?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor, which provides cost and best-practice checks account by account.
AWS Network Manager (global networks), which centrally visualizes topology and monitors transit gateways, Direct Connect, VPN, and on-premises sites and devices across accounts and Regions.
Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights, which monitors application-layer health for a single application stack.
AWS Config, which records configuration changes on individual resources over time.
explanation: AWS Network Manager (global networks) is purpose-built to register transit gateways, Direct Connect connections, VPN connections, and on-premises devices and sites into a single global network with a central topology view and CloudWatch-based event monitoring across Regions and accounts. Trusted Advisor gives account-level cost and best-practice checks, not a network topology view. CloudWatch Application Insights targets application health, not the underlying hybrid network topology. AWS Config tracks configuration history for individual resources rather than providing a unified network map.

stem: A network engineer wants to verify whether a transit gateway's route tables would successfully route traffic between two attachments in a global network before any traffic is sent, but a security group misconfiguration elsewhere is a separate concern the engineer will check with a different tool. Which statement correctly distinguishes the Network Manager Route Analyzer from VPC Reachability Analyzer for this task?
options: Route Analyzer inspects security group and network ACL rules in addition to transit gateway route tables, making Reachability Analyzer unnecessary.
Reachability Analyzer only works with transit gateway route tables registered in a global network, while Route Analyzer works with any VPC resource.

Route Analyzer analyzes only the routes in transit gateway route tables registered in a global network, and explicitly does not evaluate security group or network ACL rules, so a separate tool such as Reachability Analyzer is needed for those layers.
Both tools send live test packets between the source and destination to confirm connectivity in real time.
explanation: Route Analyzer analyzes routes in transit gateway route tables only, for transit gateways registered in a global network, and explicitly does not evaluate security group or network ACL rules, so a network-ACL or security-group check is a genuinely separate concern handled by Reachability Analyzer or VPC Flow Logs. Route Analyzer does not inspect security group or NACL rules, so the first option is backwards. The second option has the tools' scopes reversed: Reachability Analyzer works with VPC-level resources such as instances and load balancers, while Route Analyzer is the transit-gateway-focused tool. Neither tool sends live packets; both perform a static, configuration-based analysis.

stem: A network operations team wants to proactively detect when a Direct Connect connection's utilization is approaching its provisioned capacity, so they can order additional capacity (such as a LAG or another connection) before congestion occurs. Which approach is BEST?
options: Wait for on-premises application teams to report slow performance, then investigate the Direct Connect connection manually.
Rely solely on the Direct Connect console's connection State column, checked manually once a week.
Enable AWS Config rules on the Direct Connect connection resource to detect high bandwidth usage.
Create CloudWatch alarms on Direct Connect connection metrics such as ConnectionBpsEgress and ConnectionBpsIngress, with thresholds set below the provisioned capacity.
explanation: Direct Connect publishes CloudWatch metrics such as ConnectionBpsEgress and ConnectionBpsIngress for bandwidth utilization, alongside connection and BGP peer state; setting alarms with thresholds below provisioned capacity gives proactive notice to add capacity before congestion hits. Waiting for user complaints is reactive, not proactive. Manually checking the console's State column shows connection up/down status, not bandwidth trend, and is not automated. AWS Config tracks configuration changes to resources, not real-time bandwidth utilization metrics, so it is not the tool for this.

stem: A team wants an automated alert the moment either tunnel of a Site-to-Site VPN connection goes down, rather than discovering it from a user complaint. Which CloudWatch configuration achieves this?
options: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the VPN connection's TunnelState metric that triggers when the value drops below the UP threshold.
Create an AWS Config rule that checks the VPN connection's tags once per day.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the customer gateway's network interface.
Rely on the Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit's failover test to detect VPN tunnel outages.
explanation: Site-to-Site VPN publishes a TunnelState CloudWatch metric (1 for UP, 0 for DOWN) per tunnel; an alarm that fires when TunnelState drops below the UP threshold gives near-real-time, automated notification of an outage. An AWS Config rule checking tags has nothing to do with tunnel operational state. VPC Flow Logs capture ENI-level IP traffic inside a VPC, not the health state of a VPN tunnel, and a customer gateway is an on-premises device, not a monitorable AWS ENI. The Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit's failover test is a DX-specific, manually triggered verification, not a VPN monitoring capability.

stem: A security team wants to run a third-party intrusion detection appliance that inspects a copy of production traffic for a fleet of EC2 instances, without adding any component into the actual production traffic path and without installing an agent on each instance. Which capability BEST fits this need?
options: AWS Network Firewall, inserted inline in every application subnet's route table.
VPC Traffic Mirroring, which copies traffic from each instance's elastic network interface to a mirror target such as another ENI or a Network Load Balancer fronting the IDS fleet.
VPC Flow Logs delivered to Amazon S3 for offline batch analysis.
A software agent installed on each EC2 instance that forwards a copy of its traffic to the IDS appliance.
explanation: Traffic Mirroring copies traffic directly from a source elastic network interface to a mirror target, such as another ENI or a fleet behind a Network Load Balancer or Gateway Load Balancer, giving the IDS appliance an out-of-band copy of traffic with no agent required and with production traffic continuing on its original path unmodified. Network Firewall sits inline in the traffic path by design, the opposite of adding no component into the production path. Flow Logs record IP metadata, not full packet copies, and are unsuitable for deep packet inspection by an IDS appliance. Installing an agent directly contradicts the without-installing-an-agent requirement.

stem: A private virtual interface's BGP session repeatedly establishes and then drops (flaps) shortly after. The on-premises router configuration was recently changed to add MD5 authentication, but the corresponding key was not updated on the AWS side of the virtual interface. Which outcome BEST matches this situation, and how should the team confirm it?
options: The virtual interface's data-plane traffic continues normally because BGP authentication failures never affect an already-established virtual interface.
The mismatch only affects public virtual interfaces, never private virtual interfaces, so this is not the root cause.

A BGP MD5 key mismatch commonly causes the BGP peering session to fail to establish or to flap; the team should check the virtual interface's BGP peer state and update the matching authentication key on the virtual interface configuration.
MD5 authentication key mismatches only cause a one-time failure and then automatically resolve themselves without any configuration change.
explanation: A BGP MD5 authentication key mismatch between the on-premises router and the AWS side of a virtual interface is a common cause of a BGP session that fails to establish or that flaps; the fix is to check the virtual interface's BGP peer state through the console or CloudWatch and ensure the authentication key matches on both sides. Without an established BGP session routes are not exchanged, so the data plane is affected, not immune. MD5 authentication applies to private and transit virtual interfaces just as it can to public ones; it is not restricted to a single VIF type. A persistent configuration mismatch does not resolve itself without a corresponding configuration change.
